intro: A tenor decides that if life is only a dream he will stay drunk through the spring, and a solo violin plays the bird that tries to tell him it has arrived. Follow the fast drinking music, the hushed bird episode in the middle, and the drinking music coming back to silence it.
question: How does a scherzo make a joke out of despair, and what happens when the joke is interrupted?

sections.label: A′ · Tempo I — the cup refilled
sections.mNote: drinking tempo returns; the bird’s solo violin is gone

cues.title: The second scherzo
cues.text: Der Trunkene im Frühling is the cycle’s second scherzo, marked Allegro. Keck, aber nicht zu schnell — bold, but not too fast. Winds, horns and a trumpet open without strings, and the tenor enters almost at once: “Wenn nur ein Traum das Leben ist, warum denn Müh und Plag?”
cues.evidence: The first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; IMSLP #20582, printed p. 81) gives the tempo marking and shows the strings silent until rehearsal figure 1, with the tenor entering in the fifth bar. The recording begins at about −15 dB with no fade-in.

cues.title: A key that will not stay put
cues.text: While the tenor drinks “bis ich nicht mehr kann” — until he can drink no more — the harmony lurches. The printed key signature changes every few bars, and the audio’s key estimate wanders through E minor, F major, D minor, G minor and B♭ major in the first minute.
cues.evidence: Local key estimates read E minor, F major, D minor, G minor, D major, E minor and B♭ major in successive 5-second windows from 0:00 to 0:50. The Mahler Foundation’s page for this song notes key signatures changing as often as every few measures, and the score shows this.

cues.title: Li Bai wakes from drink
cues.text: The poem began as Li Bai’s “Feelings on waking from drunkenness on a spring day”. It reached Mahler through the Marquis d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s French (“Un jour de printemps”), Hans Heilmann’s German and Bethge’s rhymed version. Its opening thought — life is a great dream, so why toil? — is Li Bai’s.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Der Trunkene im Frühling page (http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Trunkene.htm), prints the Chinese poem’s translation and the French, Heilmann and Bethge versions; Edwin K. C. Li, JRMA 150/2 (2025), fn 3 lists “Chunri zui qi yanzhi” as the generally agreed source.

cues.title: Noch ruhiger: the bird
cues.text: After the tenor stumbles home and “schläft wundervoll”, the fast music stops. Around 1:34 comes Noch ruhiger — still calmer — in A major: a solo violin, trilling flutes and soft strings, with the harp soon joining, as he hears “ein Vogel singt im Baum”, a bird singing in the tree.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 1:34 (0.54), 1:40 (0.63), 1:46 (0.66) and 1:54 (0.72) follow a level dip near 1:20–1:30, and key estimates read A major or A minor with higher correlation (0.82–0.90) at 1:50–2:00. Noch ruhiger, the solo violin and the harp are in the score (printed p. 86).

cues.title: Is it spring? A dream
cues.text: At Rit. and Langsam the tenor asks the bird whether spring has come: “mir ist, mir ist als wie im Traum.” The orchestra thins to a harp, a solo violin and a few solo strings, with low winds beneath, and the pulse almost stops.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 2:06 (0.89) with level near −14 to −15 dB and onset density about 2.0–2.6 per second at 2:00–2:05, the sparsest stretch of the first half. The score marks Rit. and Langsam with harp, solo violin and solo strings (printed p. 87).

cues.title: The bird says yes
cues.text: Tempo I subito, and the bird answers: “Ja! Ja!” Woodwind trills, a muted trumpet and the solo violin’s high harmonics chirp together, and the tenor repeats that spring has arrived overnight: “der Lenz ist da, sei kommen über Nacht.”
cues.evidence: From 2:20 the level rises to about −8 dB, onset density reaches 4.8–6.4 per second and brightness peaks near 2,100 Hz; the key estimate moves from F major through F minor to C♯ major by 2:35. The score has the muted trumpet, the violin harmonics and the repeated “Ja!” (printed pp. 88–89).

cues.title: Face to face with nothing
cues.text: In July 1908, composing again with difficulty, Mahler wrote to Bruno Walter that he had “lost all the clarity and reassurance” he had ever won and stood “vis-à-vis de rien”. A poem calling life a dream and spring an irrelevance met a composer whose doctors had forbidden exertion.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s Universal Edition introduction quotes the letter of 18 July 1908 and his doctors’ restrictions: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Zögernd, ganz langsam
cues.text: The music sinks into five flats — D♭, which the audio reads as C♯ major — marked Zögernd (hesitating) and Ganz langsam (very slowly). Here Mahler replaced Bethge’s “I sigh, deeply moved” with his own line, “Aus tiefstem Schauen lausch’ ich auf”: out of deepest looking, I listen.
cues.evidence: Key estimates read C♯ major (0.63–0.81) from 2:35 to 3:10, and 3:00 has the music’s lowest brightness (about 1,000 Hz) and onset density (0.8 per second). The score (printed pp. 89–90) shows five flats and the markings; the Mahler Foundation’s footnote and the Mahler Archives page give Bethge’s line and Mahler’s.

cues.title: Cup refilled, bird forgotten
cues.text: At 3:16, the strongest boundary in the song, the first tempo snaps back with the mutes off: “Ich fülle mir den Becher neu und leer’ ihn bis zum Grund.” Harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos jolt the song back to drinking, and the loudness climbs towards the loudest minute of the song.
cues.evidence: Novelty 1.00 at 3:16, the highest in the report; level rises from −17.6 dB at 3:10 to −4.3 dB at 3:25, and 3:25, 3:35 and 3:40 are among the five loudest windows. The score marks Dämpfer ab! and Tempo I subito at figure 10, and the climax at figure 11 (printed pp. 91–92).

cues.title: Moon on the black sky
cues.text: At the climax the tenor sings until the moon shines “am schwarzen Firmament”. Harp glissandi sweep, strings play harmonics, and Molto rit. stretches the last syllables before a snap back to tempo. After it, the level falls by about ten decibels.
cues.evidence: The loudest window is 3:40 (−3.1 dB) and the level drops to −11 dB at 3:45 and −14.3 dB at 3:50. The score at figure 11 has harp glissandi, flageolet strings and Molto rit. (printed p. 92).

cues.title: A tenor who left the stage
cues.text: Carl Martin Öhmann, born in Sweden in 1887, sang in Berlin until 1937 and then mainly in concerts; later he taught Nicolai Gedda and Martti Talvela. At fifty-two he sang this performance in Amsterdam, five weeks into the Second World War and seven months before Germany invaded the neutral Netherlands.
cues.evidence: History of the Tenor (Carl Martin Öhman) for Berlin to 1937 and his pupils; the Internet Archive item description for the concert date and the 10 May 1940 invasion: https://archive.org/details/06-das-lied-von-der-erde-mahler-concertgebouw-amsterdam-carl-schuricht-5.-x.-193

cues.title: Allegro: let me be drunk
cues.text: The tenor’s last line is “Was geht mich denn der Frühling an! Laßt mich betrunken sein!” — what is spring to me? let me be drunk. A Rit. leads to a short ff Allegro in A major, woodwind and string runs tumbling to the final chord.
cues.evidence: Level stays between about −5 and −10 dB from 4:00 to 4:25, and the key estimates read A minor or A major (0.61, 0.48) at 4:20–4:25. The score marks Rit. and Allegro at figure 14 with ff runs (printed pp. 95–96).

cues.title: After the last chord
cues.text: The music ends near 4:28, and the file continues for about twenty seconds of low-level sound. Around 4:35 a brief rise appears in the level trace before the final fade; what causes it is not identified here. Listen for the song’s decay and for what follows it.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −9.7 dB at 4:25 to −28.3 dB at 4:30, rises to −15.3 dB at 4:35 and falls to −33.6 dB at 4:40 and −63.6 dB at 4:45. The report’s pitch estimates cannot identify the cause of the 4:35 rise, so none is claimed.

transitions.title: Falling asleep into the bird’s song
transitions.how: The tenor’s “schlafe wundervoll” (sleeps wonderfully) ends on a held note, the loud trumpets and horns drop out and the fast tempo stops. Noch ruhiger (“still calmer”) begins in A major with trilling flutes and a solo violin above soft strings, and the harp soon joins. The same words are about falling asleep and waking: the orchestra goes quiet exactly where the tenor does, so the bird is heard from inside his drowsiness.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 1:34–1:54 (0.54–0.72) after a level dip at 1:20–1:30, and key estimates reading A major or A minor with correlation up to 0.90 at 1:50–2:00. The held note, Noch ruhiger, solo violin, flute trills and harp are read from printed pp. 85–86 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Hesitation, then the cup refilled
transitions.how: After the bird’s “spring has come overnight” the music sinks into D♭ major, marked Zögernd and Ganz langsam with muted strings. Then Etwas fließender (somewhat flowing) quickens the pulse, the strings’ mutes are called off (Dämpfer ab!), and Tempo I subito arrives with harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos. The tenor’s “Ich” is the pick-up: the drinker interrupts the bird’s news by refilling his cup.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −17.6 dB at 3:10 to −4.3 dB at 3:25 and the strongest boundary of the song is at 3:16 (1.00). The tempo markings, mutes and instrumentation are read from printed pp. 90–91 of the 1912 full score.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, V. Der Trunkene im Frühling, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: IMSLP #20582; printed pp. 81–96. Entry times are proportioned between the audio boundaries at 1:34, 2:06, 2:20, 3:16 and 4:20 and are approximate; which edition the 1939 orchestra used is not documented.

timeline.note: Oboes and clarinets trill over horn and trumpet figures; the strings are silent.
The tenor enters over the winds and brass.
Strings join in pizzicato and arco as the tenor asks why toil and trouble.
Triangle and trumpet join the full band for “Ich trinke, bis ich nicht mehr kann”.
Noch ruhiger: the solo violin and trilling flutes picture the bird, with harp and soft strings beneath.
Langsam: harp, solo violin and a few solo strings, with low winds beneath the tenor’s question.
The bird answers “Ja!”: woodwind trills, a muted trumpet, triangle and the solo violin’s harmonics.
Zögernd, ganz langsam: muted strings, horns and bassoons under the tenor’s “Aus tiefstem Schauen”.
Tempo I subito: harp arpeggios and pizzicato cellos as the cup is refilled.
The full orchestra at the climax, with harp glissandi and flageolet strings.
Quieter again as he falls asleep: solo violin returns with winds and strings.
Allegro tutti: ff woodwind and string runs carry the song to its last chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Label

fields.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
